The flickers from different parts of the disk average out. That's a handy trick: if a bright dot shines steadily, there's a good chance it's a planet. title: Auroras Happen at Both Ends of the Earth
hook_line: Auroras happen at both ends of the Earth.
full_voiceover: Auroras happen at both ends of the Earth. Many people know the northern lights, but the southern lights are just as real, around the Antarctic region. They start with the Sun, which constantly sends out a stream of charged particles called the solar wind. Earth's magnetic field steers many of those particles toward the polar regions, where they slam into our upper atmosphere. When they hit oxygen and nitrogen, those gases glow. Oxygen often gives green, and sometimes red at higher altitudes. Nitrogen can add blue and purple tints, which is why the edges of some displays look violet. During big solar storms, auroras can reach much farther from the poles, and phone cameras often catch colors our eyes miss. Northern or southern lights: which would you travel to see? Comment below.
